system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with a history of endometriosis and bipolar disorder was admitted for acute-on-chronic left lower quadrant pain radiating to the rectum and left leg, consistent with an endometriosis flare. Initial presentation included tachycardia and severe pain requiring IV analgesics. CT imaging showed a small hemorrhagic ovarian cyst but no acute surgical or infectious findings. Pain was controlled with IV then oral medications, including increased gabapentin and addition of tizanidine. She received a Lupron injection and was started on norethindrone for long-term management. The hospital course was uncomplicated, and she was discharged home on day two in stable condition with follow-up arranged.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. You’re here for severe left lower abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same pain I had last week. It’s sharp, on the left side, goes down to my groin. I’ve tried all my meds—tramadol, ibuprofen, gabapentin—but nothing helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned nausea too, but no vomiting, fever, or urinary symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just nausea. No fever. And I’m not on my period right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your vitals are stable now. We checked your labs and found your potassium is low—3.0—so we’ll give you some replacement. It could be contributing to muscle cramps or weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so weak? I just want to sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, yes. We’re also watching your pain. You got some medications in the ER—dilaudid, ketorolac—but you’re still uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better than earlier, but still bad. I can’t function. I just need something to work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll keep managing your pain with your regular meds. We also did a pelvic ultrasound, and good news—it looks normal. No cysts or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it’s the same pain as last time. Why does it keep coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of endometriosis, this seems like a flare-up. Even if the scan is normal, the pain can still be real and severe. We’re not seeing any new surgical issues, so we’ll focus on medical management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your morning labs. Your potassium is now 4.4—much better. Your blood count shows mild anemia, but it’s not new or severe enough to explain the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anemia? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s mild and stable. But your OB/GYN should check it out as part of your ongoing care. It’s something to follow up on, not an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain has improved, and your exam is much better—no tenderness now. We’re going to discharge you soon. You’ll stay on all your usual medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing changed? What if it happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing the same plan because it’s the best we have right now. Your gabapentin and tizanidine were recently increased, which helps with nerve and muscle pain. But yes, if this keeps happening, your OB/GYN may consider other options, like a pain management referral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment with them in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Please keep that. They’ll help coordinate long-term care. We’re also sending a note to your psychiatrist to keep an eye on how you’re coping—chronic pain can affect mood, and vice versa.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s been tough. You’re stable now—alert, walking, pain much improved. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You can go home in about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another ultrasound or blood test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need now. The ultrasound was normal, and your labs are improving. But your OB/GYN might order more tests during your follow-up, especially for the anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back before my appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your PRN meds as prescribed—tramadol, ibuprofen. If it’s unmanageable, you can return to the ER. But try to reach your OB/GYN or psychiatrist first. They know your history best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll call them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing by staying connected to your care team. Take care, and I hope you feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with a history of endometriosis, bipolar disorder, and chronic pelvic pain was admitted for acute-on-chronic left lower quadrant pain, similar to a recent flare one week prior. She presented with severe pain and nausea, unresponsive to home medications, and was found to have mild hypokalemia and normocytic anemia. A transvaginal ultrasound showed no acute abnormalities. Pain was managed with continued home medications, including gabapentin, tizanidine, tramadol, and lidocaine patch. Her potassium normalized, pain improved, and she was discharged home in stable condition after approximately 12 hours with follow-up scheduled with her OB/GYN and outpatient plans to evaluate her anemia.
